Weighted Emulators with Local Heaviest Edges Stretch for Undirected Graphs
Liam Roditty, Ariel Sapir

Abstract
We introduce a generalized family of OPEN ( 2 ⋅ ⌊ k 2 ⌋ − 1 , 2 ⋅ ⌈ k 2 ⌉ ⋅ W 1 + max { 0 , 2 ⋅ ( ⌈ k 2 ⌉ − 2 ) } ⋅ W 2 ) \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil\cdot W_{1}+\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2}}\right)}}\right\}\cdot W_{2}}}\right) -emulators with OPEN O ~ ​ ( n 1 + 1 k CLOSE ) \tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right) edges, for any k ∈ ℕ k\in\mathbb{N} , where W i W_{i} is the i th i^{\textnormal{th}} heaviest edge on a shortest path between two vertices. Our construction generalizes the + 2 ​ W 1 +2W_{1} -spanner of size OPEN O ~ ​ ( n 3 2 CLOSE ) \tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{3}{2}}}}\right) and the + 4 ​ W 1 +4W_{1} -emulator of size OPEN O ~ ​ ( n 4 3 CLOSE ) \tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right) , both by Elkin, Gitlitz and Neiman [DISC’21 and DICO’23]. When k k is even, these are ( k − 1 , k ⋅ W 1 + ( k − 4 CLOSE ) ⋅ W 2 ) \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1,k\cdot W_{1}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-4}}\right)\cdot W_{2}}}\right) -emulators and when k k is odd, these are OPEN ( k − 2 , ( k + 1 CLOSE ) ⋅ W 1 + ( k − 3 CLOSE ) ⋅ W 2 ) \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-2,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k+1}}\right)\cdot W_{1}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-3}}\right)\cdot W_{2}}}\right) -emulators. Our framework not only expands known constructions for weighted graphs but also yields an improved stretch over state of the art emulators and spanners for unweighted graphs within a specific distance regime. In particular, for all vertex pairs separated by a distance of OPEN δ ≤ O ​ ( 3 k 2 CLOSE ) \delta\leq O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3^{k^{2}}}}\right) , our construction improves upon the seminal additive OPEN + O ~ ​ ( δ 1 − 1 k CLOSE ) +\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta^{1-\frac{1}{k}}}}\right) -emulator of size OPEN O ~ ​ ( n 1 + 1 2 k + 1 − 1 CLOSE ) \tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{2^{k+1}-1}}}}\right) by Thorup and Zwick [SODA’06].



Contents

Introduction

When the edge set of a graph is large, directly working with the graph can become computationally expensive. One way to alleviate this is by compressing the graph while preserving critical properties, like distances. This compression helps reduce the computational load and improve the efficiency of algorithms. In particular, one form of compression that has gained attention is the concept of
emulators
, in which the vertex set remains unchanged, but edges can be added or removed, as long as the distance between any two vertices in the modified graph remains within a specified range.

Let
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E}}\right)
be an unweighted graph and denote by
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
the distance between two vertices
u,v\in V
. An
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-emulator
H=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,F,w_{H}}}\right)
is a weighted graph with the same vertex set
V
, an auxiliary edge set
F\subseteq V\times V
and a weight function
w_{H}:F\rightarrow\mathbb{R^{+}}
, such that, for any
u,v\in V
:

\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right),\alpha\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\beta}}\right]

In other words:
\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
lies within a range bounded by the original distance
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
, up to a
multiplicative stretch
of
\alpha
and an
additive stretch
of
\beta
. Two special cases of emulators are a
multiplicative emulator
, denoted as an
\alpha
-emulator, where
\beta=0
, and an
additive emulator
, denoted as a
+\beta
-emulator, where
\alpha=1
. The general case is referred to as a
mixed emulator
, having both multiplicative and additive stretches.

A closely related object is the
spanner
, a restricted variant of an emulator that is required to be a subgraph of the original graph:
F\subseteq E
. A central question in this regime is what is the proper trade-off between the stretch
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
of an emulator or a spanner and its size
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|F}}\right|
.

This size-stretch trade-off is fundamentally tied to the
girth
of a graph. According to
Erdős’ girth conjecture

[
20
]
for any
k\geq 1
there are graphs with
\tilde{\Omega}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
edges and girth
2k+1
. In such graphs, removing any edge would increase the distance between its endpoints from
1
to at least
2k
. Any
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-emulator or spanner for such graphs for which
\alpha+\beta\leq 2k-1
must retain all original edges. This identifies
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
as a meaningful sparsity threshold.

Question 1
.

Let
k\in\mathbb{N}
. Which
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-emulators or spanners with size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
exist?

In the multiplicative regime, Althöfer, Das, Dobkin and Soares
[
7
]
presented a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2k-1}}\right)
-spanner with
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
edges. Thorup and Zwick
[
28
]
and Baswana and Sen
[
11
]
also presented such constructions. In the additive regime, Dor, Halperin and Zwick
[
15
]
presented a
+4
-emulator of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
. We observe that these spanners and emulators are optimal assuming Erdős’ girth conjecture.

Less sparse constructions include the
+4
-spanner of Chechik
[
13
]
with
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{7}{5}}}}\right)
edges and the
+6
-spanners of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
by Baswana, Kavitha, Mehlhorn and Pettie
[
8
]
and Woodruff
[
32
]
. Stretches that grow as a function of
n
(e.g.
[
17
,
23
,
22
]
) are beyond the scope of this work and are only mentioned in the tables. A summary of state of the art results is provided in
Table 1
for emulators and in
Table 2
for spanners.

While Erdős’ girth conjecture provides a baseline for tightness, it is insufficient for two reasons. First, it remains unproven for general
k\in\mathbb{N}
, making any lower bound derived from it inherently conditional. Second, it restricts us to the case where
\alpha+\beta\leq 2k-1
. For instance, the
+6
-spanners
[
8
,
32
]
of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
are not precluded by the conjecture. Resolving these gaps requires additional lower bounds.

Known lower bounds for spanners and emulators. While some present a tighter bound than others, we present all, for completeness. All lower bounds are for unweighted graphs, yet carry an implication for weighted graphs, when one assumes
\forall e\in E:w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(e}}\right)=1
.

Woodruff
[
31
]
established the first unconditional lower bounds for additive approximations, proving that additive spanners and emulators with
+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2k-1}}\right)
stretch require
\Omega\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{k}n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
and
\Omega\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{k^{2}}n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
edges, respectively. These were subsequently improved by the “additive barrier” of Abboud and Bodwin
[
2
]
, who proved that any constant additive stretch requires at least
\tilde{\Omega}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
edges. This renders the
+4
-emulator of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
of Dor, Halperin and Zwick
[
15
]

unconditionally
optimal. Henceforth, for
k\geq 4
, achieving a sparsity of
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
requires a multiplicative stretch
\alpha>1
, resulting in a mixed approximation.

Notable mixed constructions of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
include:
a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1,2k}}\right)
-spanner by Elkin and Peleg
[
19
]
, a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k,k-1}}\right)
-spanner by Baswana, Kavitha, Melhorn and Pettie
[
8
]
and a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3+\varepsilon,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3+\frac{8}{\varepsilon}}}\right)\cdot k^{3+\frac{8}{\varepsilon}}}}\right)
-spanner by Ben-Levy and Parter
[
12
]
.

Yet, these constructions consider
unweighted
graphs. Extending these results to the weighted setting introduces a fundamental conceptual challenge. Let
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)
be a weighted graph with a non-negative weight function
w:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R^{+}}
. An additive stretch with a constant
\beta

lacks scale invariance: multiplying all edge weights makes the additive stretch negligible. To address this, Roditty and Sapir
[
25
]
introduced the framework of
Commensurate Versions
. This ensures the additive stretch is relative to the weight function
w
, making the approximation meaningful regardless of scaling. We adapt their definition for emulators:

Definition 1
.

Let
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)
be a weighted graph. Consider a pair of vertices
u,v\in V
, a path
P
between
u
and
v
and a function
f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta,G,P}}\right)
. The problem of constructing an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta,G,P}}\right)}}\right)
-emulator for the weighted setting is a
Commensurate Version
of the problem of constructing an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-emulator for the unweighted setting if
f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta,G,P}}\right)=\beta
when
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(e}}\right)=1
for all
e\in E
.

Roditty and Sapir
[
25
]
also introduced the notion of
Strongly Commensurate Versions
, originally defined for algorithmic problems such as
A
ll-
P
airs
A
pproximate
S
hortest
P
aths (APASP), where the focus is on the algorithms’ runtimes. We adapt this notion for emulators, focusing naturally on their size:

Definition 2
.

Let
H_{1}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,F_{1},\hat{w}_{1}}}\right)
be an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-emulator for the unweighted setting and let
H_{2}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,F_{2},\hat{w}_{2}}}\right)
be an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta,G,P}}\right)}}\right)
-emulator for the weighted setting.
H_{2}
is a
Strongly Commensurate Version
of
H_{1}
if the problem of finding an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta,G,P}}\right)}}\right)
-emulator is a commensurate version of the problem of finding an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-emulator and
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|F_{2}}}\right|\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|F_{1}}}\right|}}\right)
.

Both definitions apply naturally to spanners as well. Early examples of strongly commensurate versions utilized
W_{\max}
: the weight of the heaviest edge in the
entire
graph. However, if a heavy edge exists but is rarely utilized in shortest paths, an approximation depending on
W_{\max}
becomes highly “loose”. To overcome this, Cohen and Zwick
[
14
]
introduced the notion

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}v
for vertices
u,v\in V
. Approximations dependent on
W_{i}
provide significantly tighter and “localized” estimations than those relying on
W_{\max}
.

Question 2
.

For which values of
\alpha,\beta
and
f
, are there
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta,G,P}}\right)}}\right)
-emulators for weighted graphs, which are a strongly commensurate version of an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-emulator for unweighted graphs?

Partial answers to
Question
2
have gained popularity in the several last years both for spanners and emulators. The
+4
-spanner of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{7}{5}}}}\right)
of Chechik
[
13
]
was adapted into a
+4W_{\max}
-spanner by Ahmed, Bodwin, Sahneh, Kobourov and Spence
[
4
]
and subsequently refined to a tighter
+4W_{1}
-spanner by Ahmed, Bodwin, Hamm, Kobourov and Spence
[
3
]
. The
+2
-spanner of Dor, Halperin and Zwick of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{3}{2}}}}\right)

[
15
]
was adapted to a
+2W_{1}
-spanner of Elkin, Gitlitz and Neiman
[
17
]
; the
+6
-spanners of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
by Baswana, Kavitha, Mehlhorn and Pettie
[
8
]
or Woodruff
[
32
]
were adapted to a
+6W_{1}
-spanner by La and Le
[
24
]
; the
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k,k-1}}\right)
-spanner of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
of Baswana, Kavitha, Melhorn and Pettie
[
8
]
was adapted to a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot W_{\max}}}\right)
-spanner by Tzalik
[
30
]
; the
+4
-emulator of Dor, Halperin and Zwick of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
[
15
]
was adapted to a
+4W_{1}
-emulator by Elkin, Gitlitz and Neiman
[
17
]
.

Table 1
and
Table 2
summarize these results, revealing a notable gap in the weighted regime: known constructions rely exclusively on either
W_{\max}
or
W_{1}
. To the best of our knowledge, no existing construction utilizes
W_{i}
for
i\geq 2
. The significance of this becomes apparent when considering a shortest path

. An additive stretch proportional to

offers no meaningful sub-multiplicative guarantee. Conversely, in this exact scenario the remaining edges must be proportionately small. An approximation utilizing

provides in such cases a strictly tighter guarantee than either

or

.

Question 3
.

Which
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(G,W_{1},W_{2},\ldots,W_{k}}}\right)}}\right)
-emulators or spanners exist, where
f
explicitly depends on at least one of the local heaviest edge weights
W_{i}
for
i\geq 2
?

Our framework addresses this fundamental gap, introducing the first explicit dependency on the second heaviest edge,
W_{2}
. We obtain a unified framework of
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil\cdot W_{1}+\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2}}\right)}}\right\}\cdot W_{2}}}\right)
-emulators with
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
edges, for any integer
k\geq 2
. More precisely, the resulting stretch depends on the parity of
k
; for an even value of
k
, these are
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1,k\cdot W_{1}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-4}}\right)\cdot W_{2}}}\right)
-emulators; for an odd value of
k
, these are
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-2,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k+1}}\right)\cdot W_{1}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-3}}\right)\cdot W_{2}}}\right)
-emulators. We emphasize that the dependence we have over
W_{1}
is linear, in contrast to other mixed approximations, such as the
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(90+\frac{120\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{k-1}\cdot W_{1}}}\right)
-emulator or the
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3+\varepsilon,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3+\frac{8}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{k-1}\cdot W_{1}}}\right)
-spanner of Elkin, Gitlitz and Neiman
[
18
]
.

In this paper we show that the
+4W_{1}
-emulator of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
of Elkin, Gitlitz and Neiman
[
17
]
is not an isolated construction, but rather the second instance (
k=3
) of our result. Starting from
k\geq 4
, we introduce an unavoidable multiplicative stretch. By
Definition
2
, any additive weighted emulator or spanner must correspond to an unweighted emulator with a constant additive stretch and the same size (e.g.
+4W_{\max}
,
+4W_{1}
or
+2W_{1}+2W_{2}
all correspond to
+4
). However, the “additive barrier” of Abboud and Bodwin
[
2
]
states that any such unweighted structure requires at least
\tilde{\Omega}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
edges. Consequently, going below the
\tilde{\Omega}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
density threshold to achieve a sparsity of
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
for
k\geq 4
cannot be done by an additive approximation.

The
k=2
instance of our framework is a special case that yields an additive
+2W_{1}
-spanner. However, for all
k\geq 3
, the construction strictly produces an emulator. This transition is motivated by a density discrepancy between the two structures. For instance, a
+4W_{1}
-emulator requires only
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
edges
[
17
]
, whereas the sparsest known
+4W_{1}
-spanner requires
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{7}{5}}}}\right)
edges
[
3
]
.

These density gaps suggest a fundamental
separation
, where an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-emulator successfully bypass the size of an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-spanner. While a proof for this gap remains a major open problem, the recurring size differences in state of the art constructions lead to the following question:

Question 4
.

For which values of
\alpha,\beta
does there exist an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-emulator that is strictly sparser than any known
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-spanner?

To better understand these discrepancies, we examine this question specifically within the unweighted regime. Two widely known results are the
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2k-1}}\right)
-spanners
[
11
,
28
,
7
]
and the
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k,k-1}}\right)
-spanner
[
8
]
, each of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
. While the
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k,k-1}}\right)
-spanner essentially “shifts” some multiplicative stretch from the
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2k-1,0}}\right)
-spanner into an additive stretch, no other intermediate trade-offs are currently known.

Our framework fills this gap by providing a new family of trade-offs of the same
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
density. In the unweighted setting, we may assume
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(e}}\right)=1
for all
e\in E
. This implies
W_{1}=W_{2}=1
regardless of the vertices in question. Our construction therefore yields a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil+\max\{0,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2}}\right)\}}}\right)
-emulator of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
. This simplifies to a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1,2k-4}}\right)
-emulator for an even
k
, and a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-2,2k-2}}\right)
-emulator for an odd
k
. There is currently no known spanner with the same stretch.

Lastly, we evaluate the performance of our framework in the unweighted regime against the most prominent constructions of the same size. When compared to the
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k,k-1}}\right)
-spanner of Baswana, Kavitha, Mehlhorn and Pettie
[
8
]
, our construction provides a tighter approximation for pairs of vertices with a distance of
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\geq k-3
for even
k
, or
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\geq\frac{k-1}{2}
for odd
k
. Furthermore, our framework strictly improves upon the
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1,2k}}\right)
-spanner of Elkin and Peleg
[
19
]
, for any
k\in\mathbb{N}
.

Implications of our result. The size is
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
and the construction time is
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
for
k\leq 4
and
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{2}{k}}}}\right)
for
k\geq 5
.

It is also interesting to compare our result to the
+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)\cdot\delta^{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1-\frac{1}{k}}}\right)}
-emulator of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{2^{k+1}-1}}}}\right)
of Thorup and Zwick
[
29
]
. To do so, observe that our result computes a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-3,2^{k+2}-4}}\right)
-emulator of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{2^{k+1}-1}}}}\right)
. While the Thorup and Zwick emulator eventually provides a better stretch for sufficiently large distances, our construction maintains a tighter approximation for all vertices within “short distance” of one another. Notably, the threshold for this range grows exponentially at a rate of approximately
3^{k^{2}}
. For
k=2
, our stretch is tighter for all pairs whose original distance is at most
70
, a threshold that expands rapidly to
5,744
for
k=3
and reaches
4,575,579
for
k=4
. This implies that for most practical values of
k
, our framework provides a superior approximation for essentially all relevant distances in the graph. We provide a comprehensive list of comparative values in
Table 6
and a visual illustration in
Figure 7
. A complete summary of our results and their implications is provided in
Table 4
.

Toolkit

Basic graph notions

Unless stated otherwise, we consider an undirected weighted graph
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)
, where
w:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{\geq 0}
is a non-negative weight function. We denote the weight of an edge by
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
, the number of vertices by
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|V}}\right|=n
and the number of edges by
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E}}\right|=m
. For any
k\in\mathbb{N}
, let
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k}}\right]=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{1,2,\ldots,k}}\right\}
.

A
path
from a vertex
u
to a vertex
v
is an ordered sequence of vertices
u=y_{0},y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{k},y_{k+1}=v
such that for every
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k+1}}\right]
it holds that
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y_{i-1},y_{i}}}\right)\in E
. The weight of a path is defined as
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(P}}\right)=\displaystyle\sum_{w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(e}}\right)}{e\in P}
. If the graph is unweighted, the weight of a path is simply the number of edges in the path
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(P}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|P}}\right|
. A path minimizing
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(P}}\right)
is referred to as a
shortest path
and its weight is the
distance
between its endpoints
u
and
v
, denoted by
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
. For a vertex
u
and a set
S\subseteq V
, we define the distance
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S}}\right)
as the minimum distance from
u
to any vertex in
S
, namely
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S}}\right)=\displaystyle\min_{s\in S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,s}}\right)}}\right\}
.

. When no explicit path is specified, we consider a shortest path between
u
and
v
that minimizes the upper-bound.

Throughout our construction, we would denote: by
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]
the distance estimate between
u
and
v
computed by our algorithm, by
\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
the distance in the emulator
H
and by
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
the distance in the original graph
G
. When providing a construction for an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-emulator
H=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,F}}\right)
, we always prove that
\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right),\alpha\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\beta}}\right]
.

Balls and pivots

For a parameter
q\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
we now consider a set
S
of vertices
s\in V
sampled randomly and independently with probability
q
each. For a vertex
u\in V
, we define its
pivot
with respect to
S
as a vertex
p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)\in S
satisfying
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)=\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S}}\right)
. That is, the pivot of
u
is the closest vertex to
u
among members of
S
. If there are several candidates we can break ties by a consistent criteria. We also associate
u
with its
ball
with respect to
S
, defined as:
ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{v\in V\,\middle|\,\,\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)<\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)}}\right\}
.

Observation 2.1

(
[
28
]
)
.

E\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S}}\right|}}\right]\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(nq}}\right)
.

Observation 2.2

(
[
28
]
)
.

E\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S}}\right)}}\right|}}\right]\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{q}}}\right)
.

Additionally, we define a classification of the graph’s edges. We associate each vertex
u
with the set
E_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\,\middle|\,\,w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)<\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)}}\right\}
. We then define the set:
E_{S}=\displaystyle\bigcup_{u\in V}{E_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}
.

Observation 2.3

(
[
28
]
)
.

E\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{S}}}\right|}}\right]\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{n}{q}}}\right)
.

By definition, every edge
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)\notin E_{S}
satisfies
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
and
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)\leq w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
. Consequently, any such edge along a

We observe that both the pivots themselves and the exact distances from every vertex to its pivot can be computed using a single SSSP computation, by introducing an auxiliary vertex connected to all vertices in
S
with edges of weight
0
.

Observation 2.5

(
[
5
]
)
.

The pivot
p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
of each vertex
u\in V
and the exact distance
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]=\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)
can be computed in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m}}\right)
time.

Additionally, we can extend the notion of a ball to consider only vertices from a certain set
A\subseteq V
. Formally, we define

ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,A,S}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{a\in A\,\middle|\,\,\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,a}}\right)<\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)}}\right\}
. Let
q^{\prime}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
be the probability for a vertex from
A
to belong to
S
.

Observation 2.6

(
[
28
]
)
.

E\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,A,S}}\right)}}\right|}}\right]\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}}}\right)
.

Hierarchy of hitting sets

We now consider
\ell
sets
S_{1},S_{2},\ldots,S_{\ell}\subseteq V
and probabilities
q_{1},q_{2},\ldots,q_{\ell}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
where, for each
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell}}\right]
, a vertex from
S_{i-1}
is independently sampled to
S_{i}
with probability
q_{i}
. It follows that
S_{i-1}\supseteq S_{i}
.

We denote
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)=p_{S_{i}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
and
E_{i}=E_{S_{i}}
. Let us consider
ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}-1}}}\right)
and
ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}}}}\right)
. As
S_{i-1}\supseteq S_{i}
, it follows that any vertex
v
that satisfies
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)<\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S_{i}}}\right)
also satisfies
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)<\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S_{i-1}}}\right)
. Hence,
ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}}}}\right)\subseteq ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}-1}}}\right)
. By the same argument it follows that
E_{i-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)\subseteq E_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
. Thus,
E_{i-1}\subseteq E_{i}
. This hierarchical structure of pivots, balls, and edge sets provides a framework for our distance estimations.

Observation 2.7

(
[
15
,
9
]
)
.

For
i<j
it holds that
S_{j}\subseteq S_{i}
and
E_{i}\subseteq E_{j}
.

For completeness, we set
S_{0}=V
and
S_{\ell+1}=\varnothing
. This proves to be consistent with the hierarchy definition we presented, and it ensures that
E_{0}=\varnothing
and
E_{\ell+1}=E
. Hence,
V=S_{0}\supseteq S_{1}\supseteq S_{2}\supseteq\ldots\supseteq S_{\ell}\supseteq S_{\ell+1}=\varnothing
and
\varnothing=E_{0}\subseteq E_{1}\subseteq E_{2}\subseteq\ldots\subseteq E_{\ell}\subseteq E_{\ell+1}=E
. Let
j\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell}}\right]
. By applying
Observation
2.1
and
Observation
2.2
:

Observation 2.8

(
[
15
,
9
]
)
.

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{j}}}\right|\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n\cdot\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{j}{q_{k}}}}\right)
.

Observation 2.9

(
[
15
,
28
]
)
.

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{j}}}}\right)}}\right|\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{j}{\frac{1}{q_{k}}}}}\right)
.

Let
P
be a path between
u
and
v
and let
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell}}\right]
. As mentioned in
Section
2.1
, an edge
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)\in P
such that
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)\notin E_{i}
provides an upper bound on the distance from each endpoint
x
or
y
to its corresponding pivot
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
or
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)
. To properly make-use of this observation, we denote by
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|P}}\right|_{i}
the number of edges in
P
that are not in
E_{i}
. If
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|P}}\right|_{i}>0
, we denote by
\overset{i}{\overrightarrow{P}}
the first edge, from
u
’s perspective, that does not belong to
E_{i}
and by
\overset{i}{\overleftarrow{P}}
the last edge, from
u
’s perspective, that does not belong to
E_{i}
.

Observation 2.10
.

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|P}}\right|_{i}=0
iff
P\subseteq E_{i}
and
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|P}}\right|_{i}=1
iff
\overset{i}{\overrightarrow{P}}=\overset{i}{\overleftarrow{P}}
.

We consider auxiliary edges, that connect each vertex to its pivot. Namely, these are
D_{i}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)\,\middle|\,\,u\in V}}\right\}
. We set
D=\displaystyle\bigcup_{i=1}^{\ell}{D_{i}}
as their union.

Observation 2.11

(
[
15
,
14
]
)
.

Let
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell}}\right]
. Then:
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|D_{i}}}\right|\in O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n}}\right)
. Additionally,
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|D}}\right|\in O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n\cdot\ell}}\right)
. If
\ell\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)
then
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|D}}\right|\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n}}\right)
.

Additionally, we consider refined balls of the form
ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}},S\textsubscript{{j}}}}\right)
for
i<j
, which are generally smaller than the standard
ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{j}}}}\right)
. By
Observation
2.9
and
Observation
2.6
:

Observation 2.12

(
[
28
]
)
.

Let
i,j\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell}}\right]
such that
i<j
. Then:
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}},S\textsubscript{{j}}}}\right)}}\right|\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\displaystyle\prod_{k=i}^{j}{\frac{1}{q_{k}}}}}\right)
.

For example, when
j=i+1
, we define

ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}},S\textsubscript{{i}+1}}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{s\in S_{i}\,\middle|\,\,\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,s}}\right)<\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{i+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)}}\right\}
. These are
the members of
S_{i}
that are closer to
u
than its pivot
p_{i+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
in the next-level set
S_{i+1}
. Our result is focused around such sets, as they may provide a finer distance estimation than what could be achieved solely with the standard sets
ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}}}}\right)
and the edge sets
E_{i}
.

Lastly, having these sets, we consider auxiliary edges from a vertex
u
to members of
ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}},S\textsubscript{{i}+{j}}}}\right)
for
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell}}\right]
and
j\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell-i}}\right]
. We define:
B_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,s}}\right)\,\middle|\,\,\exists{i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell}}\right]\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0}}\right\}}:s\in ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}},S\textsubscript{{i}+{j}}}}\right)}}\right\}
. For example, when
j=1
we consider the set
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,s}}\right)\,\middle|\,\,\exists{i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,1,\ldots,\ell-1}}\right\}:s\in ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}},S\textsubscript{{i}+1}}}\right)}}}\right\}
. This is the set of edges from
u
to any
s\in S_{i}
such that
s\in ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}},S\textsubscript{{i}+1}}}\right)
. By
Observation
2.12
:

Observation 2.13
.

Let
u\in V
,
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell}}\right]
and
j\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell-i}}\right]
. Then:
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|B_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right|\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\ell\cdot\displaystyle\prod_{k=i}^{i+j}{\frac{1}{q_{k}}}}}\right)
. If
\ell\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)
this becomes
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\displaystyle\prod_{k=i}^{i+j}{\frac{1}{q_{k}}}}}\right)
.

For a subset
A\subseteq V
, we define
B_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(A}}\right)=\displaystyle\bigcup_{a\in A}{B_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(a}}\right)}
. The size of
B_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(A}}\right)
for certain subsets
A
will be of high importance for our emulators’ size analysis:

Observation 2.14
.

Let
A\subseteq V
,
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell}}\right]
,
j\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell-i}}\right]
and assume
\ell\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)
. Then:
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|B_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(A}}\right)}}\right|\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|A}}\right|\cdot\displaystyle\prod_{k=i}^{i+j}{\frac{1}{q_{k}}}}}\right)
.

Overview

To construct our emulator
H=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,F,w_{H}}}\right)
, we utilize a hierarchy of nested hitting sets
V=S_{0}\supseteq S_{1}\supseteq\ldots\supseteq S_{k}=\varnothing
, where each set
S_{i}
defines an
i^{\textnormal{th}}
level pivot
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
for every vertex
u\in V
. At a high level, our construction proceeds in two phases:

1.

Sample each
u\in S_{i}
into
S_{i+1}
independently with probability
q_{i}=q=n^{-\frac{1}{k}}
to form the hierarchy,

2.

Construct
F
as the union of the edge sets
1
1

1

We observe that each set is of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
.
:
D
,
E_{1}
,
S_{i-1}\times S_{k-i}
for
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k}}\right]
,
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)
and
B_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}}}\right)
.

While such hierarchies are also foundational for
A
ll-
P
airs
A
pproximate
S
hortest
P
aths (
APASP
)
[
14
,
15
,
10
]
and
A
pproximate
D
istance
O
racles (
ADO
)
[
28
,
10
,
16
]
, the construction of an emulator fundamentally differs from them. APASP and ADO algorithms optimize runtime by invoking
S
ingle
S
ource
S
hortest
P
aths (
SSSP
) from small vertex sets over edge set (possibly, different) of corresponding size. In contrast, an emulator must commit to a single edge set
F
.

This commitment precludes techniques standard in APASP or ADO. For example, Cohen and Zwick
[
14
]
can “bypass” denser regions of the graph by adding auxiliary edges
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{u}}\right\}\times V
per SSSP invocation from
u
. For an emulator to commit to all such sets yields the complete cartesian product
V\times V
. A similar phenomenon appears in Dor, Halperin and Zwick
[
15
]
or in Roditty and Sapir
[
25
]
, when an APASP algorithm utilizes cartesian products
S_{j}\times S_{\ell}
in an SSSP invocation. The size of these products is proportional to the source set from which the SSSP is invoked. In contrast, emulators may commit only to one size of a cartesian product. Finally, there is an issue of the nested edge sets: invoking SSSP from a source set
S_{i}
over a specific edge set
E_{i+1}
, ensures the total complexity remains within
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{i}}}\right|\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{i+1}}}\right|
. This is most notably used by Baswana and Kavitha
[
10
]
. In the case of
i=k-1
for example, this results in
E_{k}=E
. While this is permissible in APASP due to the small size of
S_{k-1}
, an emulator attempting to replicate this step would be forced to include
E
entirely.

Consequently, identical hierarchies yield strictly weaker bounds for emulators than for APASP. For instance, the same hierarchy used to achieve the
+2W_{1}
-APASP algorithm of Cohen and Zwick
[
14
]
can only be utilized to achieve the
+4W_{1}
-emulator of Elkin, Gitlitz and Neiman
[
17
]
. This discrepancy is emphasized in the additive regime. While additive APASP permits various runtime-stretch trade-offs
[
26
,
25
,
14
]
, the
\tilde{\Omega}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
lower bound of Abboud and Bodwin
[
2
]
prohibits the existence of additive emulators.

Our approach relies on bounding distance estimations between pivots of vertices along the shortest path. To maintain the required emulator size of
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
, we can only afford auxiliary edges bridging pivots of levels
i
and
j
if
i+j=k-1
. Consequently, as
k
increases, our construction must connect increasingly higher level pivots. Since
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\geq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)
for any
x\in V
, upper bounding distances through higher level pivots inherently yields a “weaker” approximation. In other words, as
k
increases, the overall stretch increases as well. While the resulting stretch and size depends on
k
, our case analysis approach circumvents any structural dependence on
k
. Let
u,v\in V
and fix a

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}v}}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)
.

If
Case (a)
occurs,
\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)=\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
as
E_{1}\subseteq F
. Roughly speaking,
Case (b)
increases the additive stretch, while
Case (c)
increases the multiplicative stretch. For example, when moving from
k=3
to
k=4
, we increase the multiplicative stretch from
1
to
3
due to
Case (c)
. As
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{1}}}\right|=n^{\frac{3}{4}}
and we aim for size
n^{\frac{5}{4}}
, we cannot use an auxiliary edge of the form
S_{1}\times S_{1}
. We can, however, use
S_{1}\times S_{2}
, since
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{2}}}\right|=n^{\frac{1}{2}}
. While
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
and
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)\leq w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)
, we bound the distances to the second level pivots by
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)
and
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
, under additional assumptions specified later. At worst
u=x
and
w=v
, thus our upper bound is inherently restricted by
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
. Consequently, the multiplicative stretch increases from
1
to
3
.

This establishes a stretch-size trade-off parameterized by
k
. Increasing
k
improves sparsity but yields alternating penalties: an odd-to-even transition increases the multiplicative stretch by
2
, whereas an even-to-odd transition increases the additive stretch by
2W_{1}+2W_{2}
. Formalizing this alternating behavior, we derive our generalized
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil\cdot W_{1}+\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2}}\right)}}\right\}\cdot W_{2}}}\right)
-emulator.

We initially present our constructions in a simplified conceptual form without prioritizing runtime efficiency. We assume that the weight of any auxiliary edge
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\in F
that did not exist in
E
is
w_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)=\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
. Finally, all our constructions can be adapted to run in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
time. This is achieved by a two-phase algorithmic approach:

1.

Invoke an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\tau,\eta}}\right)
-APASP algorithm for certain parameters
\tau
and
\eta
, resulting in a distance estimation matrix
d
,

2.

Use these estimates to construct a sparse set of edges, resulting in an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-emulator. The weights of each edge are given by the distance estimation matrix
d
.

Main Technical Contributions

Our framework introduces two theoretical innovations. The first is algorithmic. While previous constructions utilize edges such as
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)
, these sets are primarily effective for bounding distances to second level pivots. Relying exclusively on
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)
for higher level pivots leads to a rapidly increasing multiplicative stretch as it accumulates over the levels. To circumvent this, we introduce the auxiliary edge set
B_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}}}\right)
, which allows us to bound third level pivots directly through first level pivots. By maintaining tight distance estimates at these base hierarchy levels, we prevent the rapid growth of multiplicative stretch in all subsequent levels. Surprisingly, extending this approach to higher level edge sets
B_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{j-1}}}\right)
for
j\geq 3
(e.g.
B_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{2}}}\right)
) is ineffective. Such edge sets “shift” additive stretch into multiplicative stretch, making them redundant.

The second innovation regards our proof methodology. Classifying paths strictly by edges absent from
E_{1}
ensures our
analysis remains constrained to three cases regardless of the hierarchy depth
k
. In contrast, a naive case distinction based on missing edges across the full hierarchy
E_{1},E_{2},\ldots,E_{k-1}
might appear advantageous as it provides immediate distance information to higher level pivots, however, it necessitates an escalating number of
5+6k
cases. Furthermore, it results in the same stretch bound.

Structure of the paper

As a warm-up, we review in
Section
4
the
+4W_{1}
-emulator (
k=2
) of Elkin, Gitlitz and Neiman
[
17
]
, establishing the case analysis framework for all subsequent proofs. Building on these mechanics,
Section
5
introduces a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3,4W_{1}}}\right)
-emulator (
k=3
) of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{5}{4}}}}\right)
. These results are generalized to arbitrary
k\in\mathbb{N}
in
Section
6
, yielding a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil\cdot W_{1}+\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2}}\right)}}\right\}\cdot W_{2}}}\right)
-emulator of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
. Finally, we discuss in
Section
7
the advantages of our emulator compared to the classical result of Thorup and Zwick
[
29
]
, for vertices whose distance is “short” (i.e.
\leq O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3^{k^{2}}}}\right)
).
We present a runtime efficient implementation for our weighted emulators in
Appendix
A
.

Warm-up: additive
+4W_{1}
-emulator

Input:
An undirected non-negative weighted graph
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)
.

Output:
A
+4W_{1}
-emulator.

Compute APSP

Let
\beta,\gamma\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
to be fixed later

Sample each vertex of
V
with probability
n^{-\beta}
to
S_{1}

Sample each vertex of
S_{1}
with probability
n^{-\gamma}
to
S_{2}

For every
u\in V
find the pivot
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
(respectively,
p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
)

Construct the set of edges
D

Construct the set of edges
E_{1}

Set
F\leftarrow D\cup E_{1}\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}\times S_{1}}}\right)

Initialize
w_{H}\leftarrow\varnothing

for

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\in F

do

w_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\leftarrow\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)

return

H=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,F,w_{H}}}\right)

Algorithm 1

+4W_{1}
-emulator
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)}}\right)

As a warm-up, we review the construction of the
+4W_{1}
-emulator by Elkin, Gitlitz and Neiman
[
17
]
, which yields an emulator of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
. Following the framework in
Section
3
, we assume distances are known a priori, as the final weights are defined by
w_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\leftarrow\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
for all
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\in F
.

Algorithm
1
works as follows: first, we sample vertices of
V
, with probability
n^{-\beta}
to form the set
S_{1}
. Second, we sample vertices of
S_{1}
with probability
n^{-\gamma}
to form the set
S_{2}
. For any
u\in V
, we identify the designated pivots
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
and
p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
and construct the set
D
containing all edges between vertices and their respective pivots (See:
Observation
2.5
). Utilizing these distances, we construct the set
E_{1}
consisting of edges strictly nearer than a pivot (See:
Observation
2.3
). Finally, we define
F
as the union of
D
,
E_{1}
and
S_{1}\times S_{1}
.

This concludes the description of
Algorithm
1
. Let

Lemma
4.1
,
Lemma
4.2
and
Lemma
4.3
bound the distance
\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
for
Case (a)
,
Case (b)
and
Case (c)
, respectively, after which we prove the overall sparsity is bounded by
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
.

Lemma 4.1
.

If

.

∎

We observe that
Lemma
4.2
constitutes the bottleneck for the current
k=2
construction. However, for
k\geq 3
, both
Case (b)
and
Case (c)
will emerge as the dominant bounds. We establish the emulator’s size:

Theorem 4.4
.

Algorithm
1
constructs a
+4W_{1}
-emulator of expected size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
.

Proof.

The correctness of the emulator follows from the case analysis in
Lemma
4.1
through
Lemma
4.3
. To analyze the expected size of
F
, we first note that
Observation
2.1
implies
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{1}}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1-\beta}}}\right)
and
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{2}}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1-\beta-\gamma}}}\right)
. By
Observation
2.3
, the edge sets satisfy
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{1}}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta}}}\right)
and
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{2}}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta+\gamma}}}\right)
. By
Observation
2.11
the edge set
D
contributes
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n}}\right)
edges. Finally, the product
S_{1}\times S_{1}
and
V\times S_{2}
have sizes
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2-2\beta}}}\right)
and
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2-\beta-\gamma}}}\right)
, respectively. Thus, the total size of the emulator is bounded by:

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|F}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|D}}\right|+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{1}}}\right|+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{1}}}\right|\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{1}}}\right|+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|V}}\right|\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{2}}}\right|}}\right)=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta}+n^{2-2\beta}+n^{2-\beta-\gamma}}}\right)

Setting
\beta=\gamma=\frac{1}{3}
yields the desired bound of
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
.

∎

First step:
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3,4W_{1}}}\right)
-emulator

We now present the second step (
k=3
) of our generalized framework: a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3,4W_{1}}}\right)
-emulator of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{5}{4}}}}\right)
. This construction preserves the additive guarantee of the
+4W_{1}
-emulator from
Section
4
while increasing the multiplicative stretch from
1
to
3
.
Increasing the multiplicative stretch is mandatory due to the
\tilde{\Omega}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
lower bound of Abboud and Bodwin
[
2
]
. Notably, this construction introduces an additional set of auxiliary edges
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)
, that plays a crucial role in the subsequent stages of our generalized framework.

Algorithm
2
uses three parameters
\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
such that a vertex from
S_{i-1}
has probability
n^{-\beta_{i}}
to be sampled to
S_{i}
, for
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[3}}\right]
. For completeness, we set
S_{0}=V
and
S_{4}=\varnothing
, hence
E_{4}=E
. After sampling, we identify the pivots
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
,
p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
and
p_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
for every
u\in V
, forming the auxiliary edge sets
D
and
E_{1}
. Additionally, we construct the set of edges
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)
from vertices to members of their bunch (See:
Section
2.3
).

Input:
An undirected non-negative weighted graph
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)
.

Output:
A
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3,4W_{1}}}\right)
-emulator.

Compute APSP

Let
\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
to be fixed later

Set
S_{0}\leftarrow V

for

i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[3}}\right]

do

Sample each vertex of
S_{i-1}
with probability
n^{-\beta_{i}}
to
S_{i}

For every
u\in V
find the pivot
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)

Construct the set of edges
D_{i}

Set
S_{4}\leftarrow\varnothing

D\leftarrow\displaystyle\bigcup_{i=1}^{3}{D_{i}}

Construct the set of edges
E_{1}

Construct the set of edges
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)

Set
F\leftarrow D\cup E_{1}\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}\times S_{2}}}\right)\cup B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)

Initialize
w_{H}\leftarrow\varnothing

for

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\in F

do

w_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\leftarrow\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)

return

H=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,F,w_{H}}}\right)

Algorithm 2

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3,4W_{1}}}\right)
-emulator
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)}}\right)

We set
F
to be
D\cup E_{1}\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}\times S_{2}}}\right)\cup B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)
and the weight
w_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
to be
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
for
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\in F\setminus E
. This concludes
Algorithm
2
. To argue that
H=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,F,w_{H}}}\right)
is a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3,4W_{1}}}\right)
-emulator we consider arbitrary
u,v\in V
and fix a

:

It follows that
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq 2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
. Recall that
S_{1}\times S_{2}\subseteq F
. Hence:

\displaystyle\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right),y}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$u\hbox to10.36pt{\vbox to4.99pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 1.56577pt\lower-0.7884pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {

Finally, we address
Case (c)
, where we have at least two edges to “bridge over”.
Utilizing
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)
to bound distances to third level pivots is inefficient, hence we use
B_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}}}\right)
. While we get, unavoidably, a multiplicative stretch, we have two edges that can be used as an upper bound, hence we can use
W_{2}
instead of
W_{1}
.

p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\in ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{2}}}\right)

p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\in ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{2}}}\right)
by the definition of
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)
, it follows that
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),w}}\right)\in B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\subseteq B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)\subseteq F
. Therefore:

\displaystyle\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),w}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

2.

Case (c
2
)
:
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{2}}}\right)
and
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{2}}}\right)

It follows that
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
. Recall that
S_{1}\times S_{2}\subseteq F
. Therefore:

\displaystyle\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right),w}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

∎

Having proven the three cases, we conclude with the size of the emulator:

Theorem 5.4
.

Algorithm
2
constructs a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3,4W_{1}}}\right)
-emulator of expected size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{5}{4}}}}\right)
.

Proof.

5.1
is trivial. We consider the upper bounds of

and

+6W_{1}

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3,4W_{2}}}\right)
, respectively. Both of these are smaller than
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3,4W_{1}}}\right)
. Hence, we conclude that for any

.

We now analyze the expected size of the emulator. By
Observation
2.1
, it follows that
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{1}}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1-\beta_{1}}}}\right)
,
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{2}}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}}}}\right)
and
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{3}}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}-\beta_{3}}}}\right)
. Hence, the product
S_{1}\times S_{2}
contributes
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2-2\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}}}}\right)

edges; the set
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)
, it contributes at most
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta_{1}}+n^{1+\beta_{2}}+n^{1+\beta_{3}}}}\right)
edges due to
Observation
2.14
; the set
D
contributes
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n}}\right)
edges due to
Observation
2.11
; finally,
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{1}}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta_{1}}}}\right)
by
Observation
2.3
. The total size of
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|F}}\right|
is therefore:

\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|D}}\right|+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{1}}}\right|+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{1}}}\right|\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{2}}}\right|+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)}}\right|}}\right)=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta_{1}}+n^{2-2\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}}+n^{1+\beta_{2}}+n^{1+\beta_{3}}}}\right)

By selecting
\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\beta_{3}=\frac{1}{4}
, the size becomes
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{5}{4}}}}\right)
.
∎

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil\cdot W_{1}+\displaystyle\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2}}\right)}}\right\}\cdot W_{2}}}\right)
-emulators

In this section we present a
(k-1,k\cdot W_{1}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-4}}\right)\cdot W_{2})
-emulator for even values
k
, and a
(k-2,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k+1}}\right)\cdot W_{1}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-3}}\right)\cdot W_{2})
-emulator for odd values of
k
. The size of the resulting emulator is
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
. When
k=3
this results in the
+4W_{1}
-emulator with
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{4}{3}}}}\right)
edges from
Section
4
, and when
k=4
this is the
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3,4W_{1}}}\right)
-emulator with
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{5}{4}}}}\right)
edges from
Section
5
.

Algorithm
3
introduces
k-1
parameters
\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\dots,\beta_{k-1}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
such that a vertex from
S_{i-1}
has probability
n^{-\beta_{i}}
to be sampled into
S_{i}
, for
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k-1}}\right]
. For completeness of our hierarchical structure, we define
S_{0}=V
and
S_{k}=\varnothing
. After sampling these sets, we identify the
k-1
pivots
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
for each vertex
u\in V
and
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k-1}}\right]
. We then construct the auxiliary edge set
D_{i}
connecting each vertex
u\in V
to its respective pivot
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
, and set
D=\displaystyle\bigcup_{i=1}^{k-1}{D_{i}}
. Utilizing the distances
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)
for any
u\in V
, we compute the edge set
E_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
and then
E_{1}
. Furthermore, extending the idea presented in
Algorithm
2
, we construct the edge sets
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)
and
B_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}}}\right)
(See:
Section
2.3
).

We set
F
to be the union of the edge sets:
D
,
E_{1}
,
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)
,
B_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}}}\right)
. In addition, we add to
F
any pair
S_{i-1}\times S_{k-i}
for
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k}}\right]
. Finally, we set the weight
w_{H}
of each edge
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\in F
to equal its exact distance
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
in the original graph
G
. This concludes the construction of
Algorithm
3
. We now show that
H=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,F,w_{H}}}\right)
is a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil\cdot W_{1}+\displaystyle\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2}}\right)}}\right\}\cdot W_{2}}}\right)
-emulator.

, similarly to the case analysis presented in
Algorithm
1
and
Algorithm
2
. For each case, we analyze the even and odd values of
k
separately.

Input:
An undirected non-negative weighted graph
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)
and an integer
k\geq 2
.

Output:
A
(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil\cdot W_{1}+\max\{0,2\cdot(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2)\}\cdot W_{2})
-emulator.

Compute APSP

Let
\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\ldots,\beta_{k-1}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
to be fixed later

Set
S_{0}\leftarrow V

for

i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k-1}}\right]

do

Sample each vertex of
S_{i-1}
with probability
n^{-\beta_{i}}
to
S_{i}

For every
u\in V
find the pivot
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)

Construct the set of edges
D_{i}

Set
S_{k}\leftarrow\varnothing

D\leftarrow\displaystyle\bigcup_{i=1}^{k-1}{D_{i}}

Construct the set of edges
E_{1}

Construct the set of edges
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)

Construct the set of edges
B_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}}}\right)

Set
F\leftarrow D\cup E_{1}\cup B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)\cup B_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}}}\right)

for

i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k}}\right]

do

F\leftarrow F\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{i-1}\times S_{k-i}}}\right)

Initialize
w_{H}\leftarrow\varnothing

for

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\in F

do

w_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\leftarrow\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)

return

H=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,F,w_{H}}}\right)

Algorithm 3

generalEmulator
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right),k}}\right)

For
Case (b)
, we first establish a crucial structural property. While our previous arguments naturally bound
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)
and
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)
, bounding higher level pivots
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)
and
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)
for
i\geq 2
requires further care. We prove that as long as the pivots of
x
and
y
avoid the respective opposing bunches at all lower levels, the distance to the
i^{\textnormal{th}}
pivot remains strictly bounded by
i\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
. Specifically:

Claim 6.2
.

Assume
Case (b)
holds. Let
i\leq k
such that for every
j\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[i-1}}\right]
it holds that
p_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,S\textsubscript{{j}},S\textsubscript{{j}+1}}}\right)
and
p_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,S\textsubscript{{j}},S\textsubscript{{j}+1}}}\right)
, then
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right),\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)\leq i\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
.

Proof.

We prove this claim by induction on
i
. For the base case, assume
i=2
. As
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)\notin E_{1}
, it follows that
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right),\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)\leq w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
. By the assumption for
i=2
, it also holds that
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{2}}}\right)
and
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{2}}}\right)
. Hence it follows that:

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{2}}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)\leq w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

By a symmetric argument

\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)\leq 2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
.
Now, assume the claim holds inductively for
i-1
. Therefore,
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right),\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{i-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(i-1}}\right)\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
. Consequently:

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$p_{i-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,S\textsubscript{{i}-1},S\textsubscript{{i}}}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{i-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{i\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Induction hypothesis\end{tabular}}}}

By a symmetric argument utilizing the premise that
p_{i-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,S\textsubscript{{i}-1},S\textsubscript{{i}}}}\right)
, we obtain
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)\leq i\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
. This concludes the proof.
∎

)

2.

Case (b
2
)
: For any
i\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil
both
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,S\textsubscript{{i}},S\textsubscript{{i}+1}}}\right)
and
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,S\textsubscript{{i}},S\textsubscript{{i}+1}}}\right)

As the above holds for any
i\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil
, consider
i_{1}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1
and
i_{2}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil
. By
Claim
6.2
, it holds that
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1}}\right)\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
and
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
. Furthermore, observe that the auxiliary edge
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)\in S_{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1}\times S_{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil}\subseteq F
, as
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil=k-1
. It hence follows that:

introduces an unacceptably large multiplicative stretch. To achieve a refined upper bound for

to the pivot’s pivots

(and symmetrically for
w
). Specifically:
