Table 5:
Several demonstrations of
Claim
6.4
for
i\geq 3
and the separate cases of
i=1
and
i=2
. The left column holds the assumptions for these specific base cases. The middle column presents the immediate implications for the distances
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)
and
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right),p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)
. The right column establishes our desired upper bounds for the distances
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)
and
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)
.

Proof.

We prove this claim by induction on
i
. As the upper bound depends on the value of
i\pmod{4}
, the induction requires four consecutive base cases. We establish the base cases for
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{2,3,4,5}}\right\}
.

We begin with the first base case,
i=2
(where
2=2\pmod{4}
). By the premise of the claim, we have
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{2}}}\right)
. Thus, we obtain:

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{2}}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)\leq w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

This matches the required upper bound for
i=2\pmod{4}
. Symmetrically, by reversing the roles of
x
and
w
and applying
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{2}}}\right)
, it follows that
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
.

For the second base case,
i=3
(where
3=1\pmod{2}
), we consider as well the additional assumption that
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{3}}}\right)
. Therefore:

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{3}}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Assumptions on $p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

Observe that the distance between
x
and the pivot
p_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
is upper bounded by routing through
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
to its respective pivot
p_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)
. Consequently, we obtain:

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Pivot definition\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Our previous conclusion\end{tabular}}}}

Overall,
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)
fits the stated bound for
i=3=1\pmod{2}
case. A fully symmetric argument holds for
w
: by exchanging
x
and
w
and utilizing the complementary assumption
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right),S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{3}}}\right)
, we directly deduce the symmetric upper bound bound
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)
.

For the third base case,
i=4
(where
4=0\pmod{4}
), we consider the additional assumption that
p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),S\textsubscript{2},S\textsubscript{4}}}\right)
. Thus:

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{4}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),S\textsubscript{2},S\textsubscript{4}}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Base case $i=2$ for $w$\end{tabular}}}}

Note that the distance between
x
and its pivot
p_{4}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
is upper bounded by routing through
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
to its respective pivot
p_{4}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)
. Therefore:

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{4}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{4}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Pivot definition\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+3w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Our previous conclusion\end{tabular}}}}

The upper bound we received fits the stated bound for the case of
i=4=0\pmod{4}
. A fully symmetric argument holds for
w
: by exchanging
x
and
w
and utilizing the complementary assumption
p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right),S\textsubscript{2},S\textsubscript{4}}}\right)
, we directly deduce the symmetric upper bound
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{4}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)\leq 2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+3w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)
.

For the final base case,
i=5
(where
5=1\pmod{2}
), we rely on the given premise that
p_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),S\textsubscript{3},S\textsubscript{5}}}\right)
. From this, we derive:

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{5}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$p_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),S\textsubscript{3},S\textsubscript{5}}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Base case $i=3$ for $w$\end{tabular}}}}

We can upper bound the distance from
x
to its pivot
p_{5}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
by routing through
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
to reach
p_{5}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)
. This yields:

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{5}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{5}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Pivot definition\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+3w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Our previous conclusion\end{tabular}}}}

This satisfies the required bound for
i=5=1\pmod{2}
. A fully symmetric argument, where the roles of
x
and
w
are replaced, and the condition
p_{3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right),S\textsubscript{3},S\textsubscript{5}}}\right)
is applied, yields the symmetric upper bound
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{5}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)\leq 2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+3w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)
.

For several explicit examples and a structural summary of these initial bounds, we refer the reader to
Table 5
. We now inductively assume that the claim holds for all indices up to
i-1
. We proceed to prove the claim for an arbitrary
i\geq 6
. By the premise of the claim, we assume that
p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),S\textsubscript{{i}-2},S\textsubscript{{i}}}}\right)
. We first bound the distance from
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
to its pivot
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)
.

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),S\textsubscript{{i}-2},S\textsubscript{{i}}}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)\notin E_{1}$\end{tabular}}}}

and its pivot

is upper bounded by the weight of the path

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)
. Hence:

\displaystyle~\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Pivot definition\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Our previous conclusion\end{tabular}}}}

Having establish the above inequality, we distinguish between the possible cases of values of
i\pmod{4}
and apply the inductive hypothesis to
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)
:

1.

Case 1:
i=0\pmod{4}
.

Since
i=0\pmod{4}
, it follows that
i-2=2\pmod{4}
. By applying the inductive hypothesis for
w
specifically at index
i-2
, we have:

\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)\leq\frac{i-2}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{i-2}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i-4}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)

Substituting this into our general recursive bound in
Equation (
6
)
gives:

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i-2}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{i-2}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i-4}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{i-2}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i-2}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)}}\right)+\frac{i-4}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)

\displaystyle=\frac{i}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{i+2}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i-4}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)

This results in the required upper bound for
i=0\pmod{4}
. A symmetric argument holds for
w
: utilizing the assumption
p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right),S\textsubscript{{i}-2},S\textsubscript{{i}}}}\right)
and replacing the roles of
x
and
w
.

2.

Case 2:
i=2\pmod{4}
.

In this case,
i=2\pmod{4}
, meaning
i-2=0\pmod{4}
. Invoking the inductive hypothesis for
w
at the
i-2
index results with:

\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)\leq\frac{i-2}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{i-6}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)

Substituting this within
Equation (
6
)
, we get:

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i-2}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{i-6}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{i-2}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i-6}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)}}\right)+\frac{i}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)

\displaystyle=\frac{i}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{i-2}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)

The upper bound we received satisfies the stated condition for
i=2\pmod{4}
. Replacing the roles of

and
w
alongside the assumption that
p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right),S\textsubscript{{i}-2},S\textsubscript{{i}}}}\right)
similarly establishes the symmetric counterpart for
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)

3.

Case 3:
i=1\pmod{2}
.

Because

is odd, the index
i-2

i-2=1\pmod{2}
. Applying the inductive hypothesis for

\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)\leq\frac{i-3}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{i-3}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i-1}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)

Substituting this into
Equation (
6
)
gives:

\displaystyle\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i-3}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{i-3}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i-1}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{i-3}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i-3}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)}}\right)+\frac{i-1}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)

\displaystyle=\frac{i-1}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{i+1}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{i-1}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)

This results in the required upper bound for
i=1\pmod{2}
. A symmetric argument holds for
w
: utilizing the assumption
p_{i-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right),S\textsubscript{{i}-2},S\textsubscript{{i}}}}\right)
and replacing the roles of
x
and
w
.

This concludes the proof of the claim.

. That is:

\displaystyle\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+w_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+w_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)+w_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right),w}}\right)+\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Auxiliary edges in $F$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle={\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Definition of $w_{H}$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)\notin E_{1}$\end{tabular}}}}

We now consider three possibilities for
i\pmod{4}
:

3.

Case (c
3
)
:

p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{2}}}\right)
,
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,S\textsubscript{1},S\textsubscript{2}}}\right)
and for any
2\leq i\leq k-4
it holds that

p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right),S\textsubscript{{i}},S\textsubscript{{i}+2}}}\right)
and
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)\notin ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),S\textsubscript{{i}},S\textsubscript{{i}+2}}}\right)
.

Observe that as we now satisfy the condition of
Claim
6.4
, we can provide an upper bound for both
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{k-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)
and
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{k-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)
, depending on
k\pmod{4}
. Additionally, we may use the auxiliary edges of the form
S_{1}\times S_{k-2}\subseteq F
. At first, we consider the auxiliary edge
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{k-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)
:

\displaystyle~\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+w_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{k-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+w_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{k-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)+w_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right),w}}\right)+\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Auxiliary edges in $F$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle={\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{k-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{k-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Definition of $w_{H}$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{k-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{k-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+2\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$u\hbox to10.36pt{\vbox to4.99pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 1.56577pt\lower-0.7884pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {

(13)

(b)

k=0\pmod{4}

Hence
k-2=2\pmod{4}
. In this case, expanding
Equation (
3
)
by
Claim
6.4
we get:

\displaystyle\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{k-2}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{k-4}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{k-2}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}\hyperref@@ii[clm:_k-1,kW1+_k-4_W2__case_c_index]{Claim~\ref*{clm:_k-1,kW1+_k-4_W2__case_c_index}}\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle={\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-4}}\right)\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+k\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Simply summing and $\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

Symmetrically, expanding
Equation (
3
)
by
Claim
6.4
bounds the distance through
p_{k-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(w}}\right)
:

\displaystyle\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{k-2}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{k-2}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{k-4}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}\hyperref@@ii[clm:_k-1,kW1+_k-4_W2__case_c_index]{Claim~\ref*{clm:_k-1,kW1+_k-4_W2__case_c_index}} for $w$ at $2\pmod{4}$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle={\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+k\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-4}}\right)\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Simply summing and $\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

Similarly to
Equation (
13
)
,
H
contains both paths, so
\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)

(14)

It should be observed that
Equation (
13
)
and
Equation (
14
)
together cover the case where
k=0\pmod{2}
. It is therefore left only to consider the case where
k=1\mod 2
.

(c)

k=1\pmod{2}

Hence
k-2=1\pmod{2}
as well. In this case, we only need to expand one of
Equation (
3
)
or
Equation (
3
)
. By
Claim
6.4
we get:

\displaystyle\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{k-3}{2}\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\frac{k-1}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\frac{k-3}{2}\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}}\right)+2w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}\hyperref@@ii[clm:_k-1,kW1+_k-4_W2__case_c_index]{Claim~\ref*{clm:_k-1,kW1+_k-4_W2__case_c_index}}\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle={\underbrace{\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-3}}\right)\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Simply summing\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-2}}\right)\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,w}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,w}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-2}}\right)\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(W_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u\hbox to10.36pt{\vbox to4.99pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 1.56577pt\lower-0.7884pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {

This covers all possible subcases
Case (c
1
)
to
Case (c
3
)
, hence we have completed the proof for
Case (c)
.

∎

Having established the distance bounds across
Case (a)
through
Case (c)
, we can now deduce the overall worst case stretch of the emulator. Since
Case (a)
guarantees the exact shortest path distance, it is dominated by
Case (b)
and
Case (c)
. By taking the maximum over these two remaining configurations, we obtain a unified stretch for all cases. To do so, we consider the parity of
k
.

Theorem 6.6
.

Algorithm
3
constructs a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil\cdot W_{1}+\displaystyle\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2}}\right)}}\right\}\cdot W_{2}}}\right)
-emulator of expected size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
.

Proof.

We now establish an upper bound for the expected size of
F
. Observe that the probability
q_{i}
of a vertex from
V
to enter
S_{i}
is
n^{-\sum_{j=1}^{i}{\beta_{j}}}
.
By
Observation
2.8
, each hitting set
S_{i}
in the hierarchy satisfies
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{i}}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1-\sum_{j=1}^{i}{\beta_{j}}}}}\right)
. The total size of the emulator is bounded by the size of the largest component:

1.

D

:

The set
D
contributes
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|D}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n}}\right)
edges by
Observation
2.11
.

2.

E_{1}

:

The set
E_{1}
is of size
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{1}}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta_{1}}}}\right)
by
Observation
2.3
.

3.

B_{1}
and
B_{2}

:

By
Observation
2.14
, the contributions of the bunch edges are
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}{n^{1+\beta_{i}}}}}\right)
and of the second-order bunch edges:

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|B_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}}}\right)}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{1}}}\right|\cdot n^{\beta_{i}+\beta_{i+1}}}}}\right)=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}{n^{1-\beta_{1}}\cdot n^{\beta_{i}+\beta_{i+1}}}}}\right)=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}{n^{1+\beta_{i}+\beta_{i+1}-\beta_{1}}}}}\right)

4.

Product sets
S_{i-1}\times S_{k-i}

:

For each
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k}}\right]
, the emulator includes the cartesian product
S_{i-1}\times S_{k-i}
. By
Observation
2.8
, the expected size of each product is:

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{i-1}\times S_{k-i}}}\right|=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\beta_{j}}\cdot n^{1-\sum_{j=1}^{k-i}\beta_{j}}}}\right)\\
=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\beta_{j}+\sum_{j=1}^{k-i}\beta_{j}}}\right)}}}\right)

To minimize
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|F}}\right|
, we balance the sizes of all edge sets (excluding the linear set
D
). The parameters
\beta_{i}
govern a trade-off: increasing
\beta_{i}
expands
E_{1}
and the bunches, but dually reduces the hitting sets
S_{i}
that determine the density of the cartesian products. To prevent any component from becoming a bottleneck, we equate the exponents by setting
\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\ldots=\beta_{k-1}=\frac{1}{k}
, ensuring every set in
F
satisfies the
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
bound. That is:

\begin{cases}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{1}}}\right|,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)}}\right|&=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta_{1}}}}\right)=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)\\
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|B_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}}}\right)}}\right|&=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta_{i}+\beta_{i+1}-\beta_{1}}}}\right)=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}+\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)\\
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{i-1}\times S_{k-i}}}\right|&=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{i-1}{k}+\frac{k-i}{k}}}\right)}}}\right)=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2-\frac{k-1}{k}}}}\right)=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)\end{cases}

It is now left to establish the approximation guarantee of
H
. Let
u,v\in V
. We first remark that
Case (a)
is dominated by both
Case (b)
and
Case (c)
(See:
Lemma
6.1
). For
Case (b)
, we know due to
Lemma
6.3
that
\delta_{H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot W_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u\hbox to10.36pt{\vbox to4.99pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 1.56577pt\lower-0.7884pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {
{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}
{}{{}{}{}}{}{}{}

Combining both we get that when

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}v
. Therefore, our construction from
Section
6
yields a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil+\max\{0,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2}}\right)\}}}\right)
-emulator of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
. This is a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1,2k-4}}\right)
-emulator for an even
k
, and a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-2,2k-2}}\right)
-emulator for an odd
k
.

To compare it to the
+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}}\right)^{1-\frac{1}{k}}
-emulator of Thorup and Zwick
[
29
,
21
]
, we parameterize our construction to match their
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{2^{k+1}-1}}}}\right)
size. By setting our hierarchy depth to the odd integer
2^{k+1}-1
, we obtain a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-3,2^{k+2}-4}}\right)
-emulator of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{2^{k+1}-1}}}}\right)
. While their stretch is
asymptotically
superior, we demonstrate that our construction yields a strictly tighter approximation for all vertex pairs up to an exponentially large distance threshold of
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\leq\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3^{k^{2}}}}\right)
. For a precise list of values, see examples in
Table 6
.

-emulator

]
.

To find these distance thresholds, we consider when:

~\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-3}}\right)\cdot\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2^{k+2}-4\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}}\right)^{1-\frac{1}{k}}

(17)

Subtracting
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
from both sides and applying the substitution
x=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}}\right)^{\frac{1}{k}}
reduces Equation
17
to a polynomial inequality. We bound the valid range for this inequality in the following lemma:

Lemma 7.1
.

Let
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-4}}\right)\cdot x^{k}-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)\cdot x^{k-1}+2^{k+2}-4
. For any integer
k\geq 2
, it holds that
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)<0
for any
x\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1,r_{k}}}\right)
, where
r_{k}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)}{k\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-4}}\right)},\frac{6^{k}-1}{2^{k+1}-4}}}\right)
is the unique real root of
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
.

Proof.

Our proof goes as follows: first, we identify the unique minimum point
x_{k}=\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)}{k\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-4}}\right)}>1
of
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
and establish that
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)<0
. Because
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
is a continuous polynomial, this guarantees the function remains negative throughout the interval
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1,x_{k}}}\right)
. To extend this range and find
r_{k}
, we evaluate
\hat{x}_{k}=\frac{6^{k}-1}{2^{k+1}-4}
to show that
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\hat{x}_{k}}}\right)>0
. It then strictly follows that a unique root
r_{k}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x_{k},\hat{x}_{k}}}\right)
exists where
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(r_{k}}}\right)=0
, guaranteeing
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)<0
for all
x\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1,r_{k}}}\right)
.

We start by evaluating the function at
x=1
:

\displaystyle f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)

\displaystyle={\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-4}}\right)-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)+2^{k+2}-4}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Definition of $f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle={\underbrace{2^{k+1}+2^{k+2}-6^{k}-7}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Simply summing\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle={\underbrace{2^{k}\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6-3^{k}}}\right)-7}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Rearranging terms\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle<{\underbrace{0}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$k\geq 2$\end{tabular}}}}

The derivative is
f^{\prime}_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)=x^{k-2}\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-4}}\right)\cdot x-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)}}\right)
. Since
x\geq 1
, it follows that
x^{k-2}\neq 0
. Therefore, setting
f^{\prime}_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)=0
yields a unique extremum point:

x_{k}=\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)}{k\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-4}}\right)}

To ensure
x_{k}>1
, we bound it from below. Because
\frac{k-1}{k}\geq\frac{1}{2}
for
k\geq 3
, we obtain:

\displaystyle x_{k}

\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{6^{k}-1}{2^{k+1}-4}

\displaystyle=\frac{6^{k}-1}{4\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k}-2}}\right)}=\frac{2^{k}\cdot 3^{k}-1}{4\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k}-2}}\right)}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{3^{k}-\frac{1}{2^{k}}}{1-\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}}

\displaystyle>\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{27-\frac{1}{8}}{1}>1

We analyze the sign of the sign of the derivative
f^{\prime}_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
around the extremum
x_{k}
. Because
x^{k-2}>0
for all
x>1
, the sign of
f^{\prime}_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
is entirely determined by its linear factor:
k\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-4}}\right)\cdot x-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)
. For
x<x_{k}
, this linear factor evaluates to a negative value, yielding
f^{\prime}_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)<0
, and for
x>x_{k}
, this factor evaluates to a positive value, yielding
f^{\prime}_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)>0
. Hence,
x_{k}
is the unique minimum point for
x\geq 1
.

Next, we evaluate, for
k\geq 2
, the function at the upper threshold value
\hat{x}_{k}=\frac{6^{k}-1}{2^{k+1}-4}
:

\displaystyle f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\hat{x}_{k}}}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-4}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{6^{k}-1}{2^{k+1}-4}}}\right)^{k}-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{6^{k}-1}{2^{k+1}-4}}}\right)^{k-1}+2^{k+2}-4

\displaystyle=\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)^{k}}{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-4}}\right)^{k-1}}-\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)^{k}}{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-4}}\right)^{k-1}}+2^{k+2}-4

\displaystyle=2^{k+2}-4>0

Observe that
x_{k}=\frac{k-1}{k}\cdot\hat{x}_{k}<\hat{x}_{k}
. As
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
is continuous, decreases over
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1,x_{k}}}\right)
, increases over
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x_{k},\infty}}\right)
and satisfies
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\hat{x}_{k}}}\right)>0
, it follows that a unique real root
r_{k}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x_{k},\hat{x}_{k}}}\right)
of
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
exists. Consequently, for all
x\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1,r_{k}}}\right)
, the polynomial satisfies
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)<0
.

∎

By
Lemma
7.1
,
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)<0
for all
x\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1,r_{k}}}\right)
. By reverting the substitution
x=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}}\right)^{\frac{1}{k}}
, it follows that
Equation (
17
)
holds for any distance
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(r_{k}}}\right)^{k}}}\right\rfloor
. We formalize this:

Theorem 7.2
.

Let
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E}}\right)
be an unweighted, undirected graph, and let
k\geq 2
be an integer.
Algorithm
3
computes a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2^{k+1}-3,2^{k+2}-4}}\right)
-emulator of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{2^{k+1}-1}}}}\right)
. Furthermore, for any pair of vertices
u,v\in V
whose distance satisfies

\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{6^{k}-1}{2^{k+1}-4}}}\right\rfloor}}\right)^{k}\in O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3^{k^{2}}}}\right)

this emulator provides a strictly tighter distance approximation than the
+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(6^{k}-1}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}}\right)^{1-\frac{1}{k}}
-emulator of Thorup and Zwick
[
29
]
.

Proof.

The correctness and size of the emulator follow directly from
Theorem 6.6
and our preceding discussion about unweighted graphs.

By
Lemma
7.1
,
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)<0
for all
x\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1,r_{k}}}\right)
. Note that
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\hat{x}_{k}}}\right\rfloor\leq r_{k}
for
\hat{x}_{k}=\frac{6^{k}-1}{2^{k+1}-4}
, hence the substitution
x=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}}\right)^{\frac{1}{k}}
yields
f_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)<0
for any distance
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\hat{x}_{k}}}\right\rfloor}}\right)^{k}
, satisfying
Equation (
17
)
.
∎

Appendix A
Runtime Efficient Construction

In this section, we present
Algorithm
4
, which is a runtime efficient algorithm that essentially constructs the same
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil\cdot W_{1}+\displaystyle\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2}}\right)}}\right\}\cdot W_{2}}}\right)
-emulator as
Algorithm
3
from
Section
6
. It has an expected runtime of
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{2}{k}}}}\right)
.
It utilizes an approach similar to Baswana and Kavitha
[
10
]
, yet is much simpler, for our usages.

Algorithm
4
differs from
Algorithm
3
by not having the exact distances
\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
apriori. To overcome this,
Algorithm
4
must compute these distances. This affects the computation of the sets that compose
F
as well. The major bottleneck is
B_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}}}\right)
which requires
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{2}{k}}}}\right)
runtime. The rest can be computed within
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
runtime.

A key observation is that
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]=\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
for certain vertices
u,v\in V
. For our usage, we would like to show that for “necessary” auxiliary edges
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\in F\setminus E
it holds that
w_{H}=\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
. In other words, we need to show that for these vertices
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]=\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
.

Remark A.1
.

As
G
is undirected, we may assume whenever a value
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]
is updated to hold a smaller value than it previously held, so does
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[v,u}}\right]
. This has no effect on the runtime.

Input:
An undirected non-negative weighted graph
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)
and an integer
k\geq 2
.

Output:
A
(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil\cdot W_{1}+\max\{0,2\cdot(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2)\}\cdot W_{2})
-emulator.

Let
\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\ldots,\beta_{k-1}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
to be fixed later

Initialize
d
as the edges’ weights and
\infty
otherwise

Set

for

for

for

For any

By definition we set

∎

For the next lemma, we consider the case where there is an edge and we are interested in the distance estimation between pivots of its endpoints.

For any

. Hence,
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),p_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right]\leq\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)
.
∎

F
.

Lemma A.7
.

Algorithm
4
requires
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{2}{k}}}}\right)
runtime.

Proof.

Let
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k-1}}\right]
. By
Observation
2.5
we can find
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
for all
u\in V
in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m}}\right)
. Also,
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]=\delta_{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)
. We construct the set
E_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
for any
u\in V
in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m}}\right)
time by simply checking whether
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)<d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]
for any neighbour
v
of
u
. Hence, constructing
E_{i}
would require
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m}}\right)
overall runtime. We assume
k\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)
, hence constructing all of the sets
E_{1},\ldots,E_{k-1}
and
D
requires the same
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m}}\right)
runtime.

To construct the set
B_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V}}\right)
, we iterate over any

and
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k-1}}\right]
. If
v\in S_{i}
we check whether
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]<d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{i+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]
. Recall that

by
Observation
2.5
. As for
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]
, if
v\in ball\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S\textsubscript{{i}},S\textsubscript{{i}+1}}}\right)
, it follows by
Observation
2.4
that
u\hbox to10.36pt{\vbox to4.99pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 1.56577pt\lower-0.7884pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {

∎

We may now conclude:

Theorem A.8
.

Let
k\in\mathbb{N}
such that
k\geq 2
.
Algorithm
4
requires
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{2}{k}}}}\right)
runtime to compute a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rfloor-1,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil\cdot W_{1}+\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}}}\right\rceil-2}}\right)}}\right\}\cdot W_{2}}}\right)
-emulator with
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
edges.

. As for the correctness, let

∎

We observe that for
k\leq 4
, the set
B_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{1}}}\right)
is not being used. Hence, the runtime, for these values of
k
, can be reduced to
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
. We therefore conclude:

Remark A.9
.

For
k\leq 4
the runtime of
Algorithm
4
is
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{1}{k}}}}\right)
.
